narrative: During the 2000s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture continued to thrive, building on the momentum of the natural hair movement that originated in the 1960s. The afro, a hairstyle created by combing out natural growth or styling with chemical curling products, remained a staple in many communities. Cornrows, a traditional style from Africa and the diaspora, were also popular, often worn in simple lines or elaborate designs. Dreadlocks, which can form naturally or be created through techniques like twisting or backcombing, became increasingly visible as a form of self-expression. Protective hairstyles, designed to minimize manipulation and environmental damage, gained popularity as women sought to care for their hair in healthier ways. Box braids, a type of protective style that originated in Africa, were also widely adopted, offering a versatile and long-lasting option. While the Jheri curl, popularized in the 1980s and early 1990s, may have faded from mainstream attention, its legacy continued to influence hair culture among Black women.
